p: Ellie finally flew in Biscuit on a cool September morning, with Abby at the controls and Claire beside her.
Walt's text marked six months gone on the one year clock.

Then came three weeks of pattern work: a worn tire caught on preflight, a gusty wind she solved by asking for a different runway, a go around from a ballooned landing, a slip with no flaps, and light signals with a dead radio.
Walt watched from the fence and held up fingers to score her landings, the way Danny had once drawn him in the notebook.
Abby signed her up for the pre-solo written and said that next time, she'd get out of the airplane.
Abby Strand. Jordan's instructor, who signed off the pattern work.
Ellie Reyes. Danny's daughter, who finally got her flight.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow, who flew beside Ellie in the back.
Walt Herrera. The safety officer at the fence.
Marisol Tran. The mechanic, who fixed Biscuit's flaps and radio jack in October.
Lourdes Reyes. Jordan's mother, still not getting in that airplane.

The pre-solo written was three pages, stapled at the corner, in Abby's block capitals, and it sat on the folding table in the briefing room on Monday afternoon with a pencil on top of it like a paperweight.

Hangar Six pre-solo knowledge test, for the 172, by Abby Strand. Thirty questions. Open book: Biscuit's POH, your sectional, the Centennial sheet. Closed book: everything else. Part one, Parts 61 and 91: what you may do alone, and what you may not. Part two, Centennial: tower, patterns, hot spots, the shelf. Part three, Biscuit: speeds, limits, fuel, emergencies, the door. Show your work on anything with a number. I'll go over every one you miss before you go anywhere without me. That's not me being nice. That's 61.87.

Jordan had come straight from a shift that had ended at seven that morning, slept five hours with the blackout curtains taped at the edges, and eaten a bowl of cereal standing over the sink. She'd taken a lot of tests. Paramedic school, the national registry, recertifications every two years with a mannequin named Gary who'd been dying since 2014. She knew how she took tests. She read the whole thing first, all thirty, before she wrote a word, the way you look at the whole patient before you touch anything.

Abby didn't watch her. Abby sat at the other end of the table with her own logbook open and a calculator, adding up something with her lips moving. Every so often she wrote a number in the margin and circled it. Jordan knew what it was without asking. Twelve hundred and something. The airlines wanted fifteen hundred.

Question nine asked what Biscuit's maximum flap extended speed was, and she had to look it up, and the POH page had a coffee ring on it in the exact shape of the mug on the briefing room counter. Question fourteen asked her to draw the Class B shelves over the field with their altitudes, and she drew them without looking, and then drew a little red ring around the 80 because she couldn't help it. Question twenty two asked what she'd do if Biscuit's door popped open on rotation. She wrote: FLY THE AIRPLANE. LEAVE THE DOOR. Then she sat looking at that for a while, because it was Danny's door. He'd never fixed it. He'd said it kept him humble.
Forty one minutes. She put the pencil down on top of the pages, the way she'd found it.
Abby graded it in green without a word. Tick. Tick. Tick. A long pause on page two. Tick. Then she wrote a number at the top, circled it twice, and turned the test around.
Good, Abby said. Now the part where it counts.

Three red marks. Question four: Student pilot. Minimum flight visibility, day, for a solo. She'd written 1 SM, thinking of Class G. Question nine: Biscuit's max flap extended speed. She'd written 110, which was the number for ten degrees only, and Abby had underlined the word ONLY in the question that Jordan had read right past. Question twenty six: Once you're signed off to solo, where may you land? She'd written ANY AIRPORT WITHIN 25 NM, which Abby had circled and written next to it, in green, who told you that.
Nobody had. She'd made it up from half a sentence in a book and believed it.
Abby leaned back. The rule says I review every one you got wrong before I let you go. How do you want to do it?

She does all three the way she'd do a missed med on a QA review: what she thought, where she got it, what the rule actually says. 61.89(a)(6), 3 SM by day. The flap page, with ONLY in bold in the POH too. 61.93(a), and the two sentences that say a solo student lands where she left unless she's been trained and endorsed for somewhere else. She writes each one on an index card. Abby watches her write the third card and doesn't say anything. Then she says, Twenty six is the one I'd have lost sleep over. A student who thinks she can land anywhere is a student who lands somewhere.

61.87 requires the instructor to review all incorrect answers before authorizing solo. Working out why you missed each one, and finding the source, fixes the reasoning instead of the answer. A student solo lands only at the airport of origin unless endorsed under 61.93.

Monday night she laid it out on the kitchen counter the way she checked the rig at the start of a shift. The plastic student pilot certificate that had come in the mail in May, white and blue, with a photo of her that looked like a hostage. The third class medical from April. Her driver's license. Her logbook, thirty eight hours, most of it in green. And the composition notebook, which wasn't any kind of document but sat on the counter with the rest of it because that's where it lived now.
A text from Abby Strand. Homework. What do you legally need with you on a local solo. And what do you bring anyway. Short answer.

She types it, with the section numbers, because she's her. 61.3 for the certificate and the ID, the medical with them. 61.51 for the logbook on cross-countries only. Logbook comes anyway. So does the endorsement page, flagged. Abby: correct. Also correct that you flagged it. Ramp checks happen. Then, a minute later: what did you bring that isn't on the list. Jordan looks at the composition notebook. She doesn't answer that one.

61.3 requires the pilot certificate and a photo ID in the pilot's possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, and the medical certificate has to be with them too. 61.51 requires the logbook and student certificate on solo cross-countries. On a local solo the logbook isn't required, but it holds the endorsements, so carry it.
Later that night, 8:15, FaceTime, and Ellie's face was too close to the camera, so it was mostly one eye and a freckle. Claire had told her. Claire told her things now. That was new.
Mom says you're going to fly Biscuit by yourself. The eye backed up and became a whole face. When you do it, can I sit in the back? I'll be so quiet. I won't even count the landings out loud.
Behind her, out of focus, Claire was doing the dishes and very carefully not looking at the phone.

Not till I'm a real pilot, El. Students can't carry passengers. When I can, you're first. Ellie chews on the inside of her cheek, which is how she thinks about everything, and wants to know if that's a rule or a Jordan rule. A real rule, Jordan tells her. The government kind. Okay. Then can I watch? Behind her the water's gone off. It's a school day, baby. Then take a picture. Jordan says she will, and after they hang up she writes PICTURE on her hand in blue Bic. Danny used to do that. She never had, until tonight.

A student pilot may not carry passengers under 61.89. Saying so plainly, with the reason, is honest and doesn't leave a promise that has to be broken. The privilege to carry passengers comes with the private certificate.

Tuesday, October 13, 7:20 in the morning, clear and cold, 2°C on the ground and the plains east of the airport gone the color of a paper bag. Bennett went by off the left wing, a water tower and a grain elevator and the interstate drawn straight through the middle of it with a ruler. Biscuit was at 6,900 and climbing, slowly, because it was the end of a long climb.
Slow flight first, then stalls. Pick your altitude and tell me why.
Jordan had done the math on the drive, at a red light on Arapahoe, and written it on the kneeboard under SHELF AT 80.

Say the floor. Ground's about fifty five hundred, plus fifteen hundred is seven thousand. Shelf at eight. Entering at seventy seven hundred. Abby nods at the altimeter, then out the window at the grain elevator. Over the field you'd have six hundred feet to work with. Out here, a thousand. That's why the practice area is out here. It's not the scenery. Clearing turns, left and right, wing up to look above. A Cherokee way off south, low, going away. Nobody else.

The ACS requires slow flight and stalls to be completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL. Over Bennett at about 5,500 ft that's about 7,000 MSL, and the Class B floor is 8,000. Entering at 7,700 leaves room for altitude loss above the floor while staying clear of the shelf.

Full flaps, 7,700, heading 090 toward a grain elevator, airspeed 50 and power at about 1,900 on the tach, which meant 1,850. The nose was high enough that Jordan had to look out the side to see the horizon. The yoke felt like it was attached to the airplane by rubber bands. Her right foot was doing more than she'd told it to.

A little bump came through, the kind you'd never notice at cruise, and the stall horn went off. A short, sour chirp from the left wing root, the kazoo Abby had warned her about. Then again. The altimeter was ticking down, 7,680, 7,670.
Abby had her hands folded. ACS says no horn. A bump's forgivable if you fix it. Fix it.

Nose down, a degree, maybe less. The horn stops in the middle of a chirp. The altimeter keeps sliding, so she brings the throttle up a hundred RPM, and it stops at 7,660 and comes back, slowly, to 7,700. Fifty three knots. She keeps it there. Right rudder, a little more. A turn to the left, 20 degrees, more power, and the horn doesn't make a sound. There. That's your number for full flaps. Fifty three. Pitch for the speed, power for the altitude. Upside down from everything you've done so far. Welcome to slow flight.

AFH: in slow flight, react to any stall warning by reducing angle of attack slightly, then add power to maintain altitude. Below L/D max, pitch controls airspeed and power controls altitude. The ACS wants no stall warning and airspeed plus 10, minus 0.

Power-off stall. Carb heat on, power back, flaps down in steps, a stabilized descent at 65 like final approach. Throttle to idle. Then, smoothly, back on the yoke, and keep coming, and the nose rose until all she could see was sky and the horn was steady and the yoke was all the way back in her lap.

The buffet came up through her seat. Then Biscuit quit, the nose dropping, and in the same instant the left wing fell away, fifteen degrees, twenty, the horizon tilting in the windshield like a picture on a wall that somebody had bumped.
Every instinct she had was in her right hand.

Forward. Not a shove, a firm push, and the horn cuts off and the buffet goes with it, and the wings are flying again. Then she rolls level, coordinated, a lot of right rudder. Then full throttle, carb heat off, and Biscuit's nose wants to come up on its own, so she holds it at a climb attitude. Flaps 20. Climbing, barely. Flaps 10. Flaps up. 7,520 on the altimeter, so a hundred eighty feet gone. Nose. Wings. Power. You did it in order, which is all I care about.

The AFH stall recovery: reduce angle of attack until the stall warning is eliminated, roll the wings level with coordinated controls, add power, then return to the desired flightpath with flaps retracted in increments. Reducing AOA is the most important step.

The October safety meeting was Wednesday at seven in Hangar Six, nine folding chairs and seven people, including Russ on Marisol's phone propped against a quart of oil. Walt stood at the whiteboard next to Danny's capitals and Marisol's, with a dry erase marker he kept capping and uncapping.

He drew a runway. Then a base leg, and an arrow on it for the wind, from behind. I read a report like this once. Doesn't matter where. Pilot with four hundred hours, nice day, tailwind on base they didn't notice. Turned final late, went through the centerline, and didn't want to steepen the bank, because everybody says don't bank steep low. So they fixed it with their feet. He drew the airplane's path curling past the runway and stopped the line in the grass. Six hundred feet. That's where it ends.
He looked at the chairs. Then at her. Jordan. You're on base, you've overshot, the runway's sliding off to your left. What do you do.

I don't steepen past thirty, and I don't fix it with my feet. If it won't line up, I go around. Walt looks at her for a while. Then he writes GO AROUND on the board, under the runway, in capitals that look a little like Danny's. Free. Every time. Costs you four minutes and your pride, and you have more of both than you think. Afterward, folding chairs, he passes her on the way to the door. Abby says soon. It isn't a question. I'll be at the fence.
The AFH: at the low altitude of a base to final turn, be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees of bank and never skid to fix an overshoot. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around.

Back on Tuesday, after the stalls, the steep turns. 85 knots, 7,700, heading 360 toward a white grain elevator on the horizon that she'd decided was hers. Clearing turns. Roll left. At 30 degrees she started the back pressure and added a hundred RPM, and at 45 she held it, the horizon lying across the windshield at a slant and the left wingtip pinned on a section line road far below.

Then she got interested in the wingtip. The bank crept to 50. The nose slid down below where it lived. The airspeed was 90, then 93, and the altimeter was unwinding, 7,650, 7,620, the VSI needle pointing at the floor.

A little right aileron and rudder, back to 40. Then the nose comes up easily, like it's been waiting for permission. 7,620, 7,660, 7,690. Back to 45, a hair of left aileron against the overbanking. She picks the grain elevator up over the nose, 22 degrees early, and rolls out, letting the back pressure off as she goes, and the needle stays on 7,700. Heading 002. Eighty low and eight fast at the worst. Inside the standard, barely. Now the other way, and watch the wings, not the road.

AFH steep turns: correct a nose low altitude loss by first reducing bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then increasing pitch with back pressure. Roll out about half the bank angle before the heading. ACS: altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 10 knots, bank within 5 degrees, heading within 10 degrees.

Wednesday, October 14, 7:40. A second short flight, ground reference work, 6,300 feet over a wheat stubble field south of Bennett. Eight hundred feet above the ground, which felt like flying through somebody's living room after a week at 7,700.

The wind at altitude was out of the west, 270 at 15, Abby said, and you could see it in the dust from a farm truck on a dirt road, a tan plume going east like a flag. Out in the middle of the stubble sat the hub of a center pivot sprinkler, a little steel tower in the middle of a huge circle. Nothing near it. Not a house for half a mile. No cows either, and Jordan checked twice, because the handbook had been weirdly firm about cows.
Pivot. Right turns, so the wing doesn't eat it. Where do you come in, and where's the bank steepest?

She comes in from the west, heading east with the wind behind her, a quarter mile north of the hub, and rolls right, fast, to 40 degrees, because the ground's going by at a hundred knots and that's no time to be shy. Coming around through south, then west, the ground slows down and she lets the bank off. 40. 30. About 15 when she's pointed straight into the wind and the hub's barely creeping by. Then she builds it back. The truck's dust shows her where she's drifting. Two laps. On the second one the hub sits pinned just off the wing strut like somebody bolted it there. That's the traffic pattern, Abby says, pleased with the hub, or with Jordan, hard to tell. Every base turn you'll ever make. Now you know why some days you overshoot.

AFH: enter ground reference maneuvers downwind, where groundspeed is highest and the steepest bank is needed. Bank decreases as groundspeed decreases toward the upwind position, then increases again. No more than about 45 degrees.
Abby signed nothing Wednesday. She said Saturday at ten, after Jordan's shift. Thursday to Friday, you sleep Friday, Saturday you're mine.

Twenty four on, forty eight off, and she'd traded a shift that week so Saturday came out clear. Then Friday at six in the morning, an hour before she got off, the captain asked who could stay over. Two people out sick. Jordan said yes because she always said yes. Forty eight hours at the station, maybe twelve of them asleep, in pieces.

At 4:10 Saturday morning they worked a cardiac arrest on a kitchen floor off Colfax, a man in his fifties with his wife holding the dog in the doorway, and they got him back. Pulse on the third check. He was talking, sort of, by the time they rolled into the ER. It was a good one. It was the kind you get maybe twice a year. She was shaking a little in the ambulance bay afterward and told herself it was the cold.

7:25 AM, the station parking lot. Thirty six hours awake, give or take. Her hands felt fine. Her head felt like a bright room with the lights on too long. The sky over the plains was perfect, clear to Kansas, no wind. Of course.
A text from Abby Strand. ATIS says calm and clear. I'm at the field at 9:30. Bring a shirt you don't love.

She types it with her thumbs in the cold: Held over. Worked a code at 4. Been up 36 hrs. I'm not flying today. Then she sits there and stares at it before she sends it, because sending it makes it real, and Saturday was going to be the day. She sends it. Abby answers in under a minute: Good. That's the best decision you've made since I met you. Tuesday 7am, sleep Monday. Then: did the code make it. Jordan writes yes. Abby writes good again, and that's it. She drives home with the window down so she stays awake and sleeps until four in the afternoon.

IMSAFE: Fatigue. After 36 hours awake, judgment and reaction time are impaired whether or not you feel it. Pushing a first solo costs a few days. Flying it impaired removes the safety margin on the one flight where no one else is aboard.
Tuesday, October 20. She'd slept nine hours. The ATIS at 7:20 said wind three four zero at six, ten miles, sky clear, temperature three, altimeter three zero one four. Under every number on the card.

7:30. Abby flew three laps with her, stop and goes, and said nothing on any of them except Mm. 7:52. They taxied back to the ramp. Abby got the logbook out, wrote for a long time on her knee, and then turned around in her seat to look at Jordan.

I told you I'd get out at the runup. Ground says no pedestrians on Alpha, so I'm getting out here. Three, full stop. I'll be on the handheld. And she's a hundred and fifty pounds lighter without me. She'll climb like she's late and float like she isn't. Take the extra knots off. Jordan pulled the mixture; Abby climbed out behind the strut and shut the right door from outside. Right one does it too, if you shut it from outside. Check mine. She headed for the fence where Walt already was, and Marisol, and the empty seat sat there next to Jordan like a person. Jordan started Biscuit again.

7:56. Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, student pilot, west ramp, taxi for departure. Ground cleared her to 35R via Alpha, and she taxied it alone, which felt like driving a car with nobody in the passenger seat for the first time at sixteen. 7:58. Runup, in the runup area on Alpha near the end of 35R. Mags, carb heat, mixture, the top latch of her own door, twice, out loud. She told ground she was ready for departure, and ground told her to hold short of 35R and monitor tower. Solid lines in front of her, nose short of them. 8:03. Cessna Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared for takeoff. 8:04. Full throttle. Airspeed alive. Fifty five. She eased back, and Biscuit, a hundred and fifty pounds lighter than Jordan had ever felt her, came off the runway like she'd been let off a leash, and there was a bang on the right side like a shotgun.

The right door was open. Three inches, then six, then back to three, flapping on the slipstream with a roar that filled the whole cabin. The checklist on the right seat went out the gap and was gone. Nobody had latched the top of the right door. Abby always did hers.

Fly the airplane. She says it out loud, which nobody can hear but her. Pitch for VY. Right rudder. The door bangs, settles, bangs. Seven hundred feet a minute up, more than she's ever seen, because there's nobody in the right seat. She levels at 6,900 on the crosswind leg long before she's used to, and the roar is just a noise now. Centennial Tower, Niner One Echo, my right door came open on takeoff. No problem, I'd like a full stop. Niner One Echo, roger, make right traffic, runway three five right, cleared to land. Downwind. Carb heat. Flaps. A normal approach, a normal landing, the door sighing shut on its own when she slows below forty. On the taxiway, stopped, past the lines, she reaches over and latches it. Top and bottom. Then she checks it again.

8:14. Second takeoff, door latched, both latches, she'd touched them like a rosary. Climbing out she noticed that she was talking. Out loud, steadily, the whole time, the way she talked a patient through a line placement. Okay. VY. Right rudder. Shelf at eight. Look left. Crosswind turn. Nobody to hear it but Biscuit.

8:19. Base, final. Same power as always, same flaps, and Biscuit wouldn't come down. Without Abby in her she floated on the descent like a paper airplane. At five hundred feet Jordan was a little high and she let it go. At three hundred feet the PAPI was four white, the airspeed was 75 instead of 65, and the aiming point blocks were going to go by underneath her.
Ten thousand feet of runway in front of her. Plenty of room. That was the thing about having plenty of room.

Throttle in. Carb heat off. Right rudder for the nose, which wants to climb the wall. Flaps 20, 10, up. Niner One Echo, going around. Niner One Echo, roger, make right traffic. Nobody tells her it was right. She knows. Downwind again, and this time she pulls a little more power abeam the numbers, because Biscuit is lighter and she's going to need less, and on final the PAPI is two and two. Over at the fence, somebody's hand comes out of a pocket. She doesn't look long enough to count.

8:31. Third takeoff. Both latches. On the climbout the low sun came across the plains off the right wing, and the whole east side of the airport went gold for a minute, the hangar roofs and the fuel truck and the grass between the runways. She didn't look long. She looked.

8:34. Downwind, 6,900, ninety knots. She was still talking. She'd stopped hearing herself do it somewhere on the second lap, the way you stop hearing a monitor until it changes pitch. Abeam the numbers. Carb heat. Fifteen hundred. Ten degrees. And then, without planning to, Okay, Danny, and she heard that one, and kept flying.

8:37. Final. Two white, two red. Sixty five knots, and she took a couple more off this time, because the airplane was light, and the numbers came up and went under the nose and she held it, and held it, and the stall horn chirped once, the good kind, and the mains touched. Then the nose. Centerline under her, the white dashes going by slower and slower.
Cessna Niner One Echo, turn right at Alpha seven, contact ground. A pause on the frequency that didn't need to be there. Nice job on the first solo.
Right at Alpha seven, over to ground, Niner One Echo. She almost said thank you, and then said it. Thank you. All the way past the hold lines. Tail too.
At the fence, Walt's hand was up. She was close enough, rolling by on Alpha, to count. Eight fingers. He held them there until she was past, and put them away.

8:46. Mixture cutoff. Mags off. Master off. The quiet came in all at once, like it always did, and for a second she just sat there with her hands on her knees and the headset still on, Danny's headset, which Marisol had handed her that morning at 6:50, in the padded bag that had been sitting in the bottom of her toolbox since March.

It was gray, older than the club loaner and heavier, with the left ear seal cracked and fixed with black tape. On the headband, scratched into the plastic with something sharp, D.R. Clipped to the cord was a clothespin, to keep it from swinging into the throttle.

Before she'd handed it over, Marisol had leaned in the left door with a shop rag and cleaned the glass on the airspeed indicator, which was already clean. She went slowly, and named the arcs as she wiped, like a checklist. White, forty one to eighty five. That's where the flaps live. Bottom of the white is where she quits flying with full flaps. Around the dial. Green, forty seven to one twenty eight. Bottom is where she quits clean. Top is as fast as you go when it's bumpy. Around. Yellow, one twenty eight to one sixty, smooth air only. Red line, one sixty. Never. She folded the rag in half. He never once saw yellow. I'd have known. He'd have told me, to brag. Then she'd put the bag in Jordan's hands and said only, He'd want it flying. I'm done keeping it in a toolbox. and gone back to her bench and started safety wiring something that didn't need it.
It fit. That was the stupid part. Jordan had braced for it not to fit.
Abby was at the wing strut before the prop stopped, with Marisol's big orange shears in her hand and her face doing something it didn't usually do. Out. Turn around.

Jordan climbed out and turned around. She'd worn her oldest station T-shirt, the one from the B shift chili cookoff, with a bleach spot shaped like Ohio. Abby pulled the back of it out of Jordan's jeans and cut. One long crooked cut across the tail, all the way, and then she held it up, a ragged navy rectangle with half of CHILI on it, and wrote on it in Sharpie on Biscuit's cowling, in block capitals: JORDAN REYES. FIRST SOLO. N4791E. KAPA. The date. Then, smaller: THREE TAKEOFFS, THREE FULL STOPS, ONE DOOR.
You flew it like somebody who's been scared on purpose before, Abby said, capping the pen. Which is the whole job. That go-around was the best thing you did all morning.

Jordan's logbook, the endorsements, in green ink. October 12: she's passed the pre-solo knowledge test under 61.87. October 20: she's had the pre-solo flight training and flown it safely. And October 20, under sixty one point eight seven, paragraph n: she's cleared to solo in Biscuit, with limits. Day VFR only, the Centennial pattern only. Wind ten knots or less, gusts no more than five over, crosswind five or less. Ceiling three thousand above the ground or better, visibility five miles. No passengers, under 61.89. And a last line, in a different pen, added in the hangar: latch both doors.

In the hangar, Marisol had already cleared a spot on the corkboard by the door, under the old whiteboard with Danny's capitals and her own. A dozen shirt tails were pinned up there from twenty years of club members, gone pale under the shop lights. Marisol pushed in four pins, one at each corner, and stepped back and looked at it for a while with her arms crossed. Then she went back to her bench without saying anything, and a minute later she was singing along to the radio, badly, which Jordan had learned was the same thing.

Walt came in from the fence with his collar up. He didn't look at the shirt tail. He looked at Jordan. Eight, he said. In case you didn't count. Then he picked up the logbook off Marisol's bench, read the endorsement page with his glasses on the end of his nose, initialed the monthly box on the inside cover, and put it down. I don't give tens.
He stopped. Looked at her over the glasses. Then he laughed, once, short, like something had gotten out before he could stop it, and walked out to his truck.

When the hangar was quiet, she took the green notebook out of her flight bag and sat on the step of Marisol's stepladder with it. She'd been reading it in order again since August, mostly. In April she had flipped through the first pages and seen one with SOLO across the top in letters an inch tall, and turned past it fast, and put a paper clip on it, and hadn't looked since. She'd been saving it. She hadn't told herself that was what she was doing. She opened it at the clip.

Danny's logbook, a page from May, eleven years ago. May 9. SOLO!!! KAPA, 152 from the school, 0.6, 3 takeoffs, 3 full stop. Instructor got out at the runup, said "three, then come get me," and walked off like it was nothing. It was NOT nothing. Talked to myself the whole time. Tower heard some of it. Apparently I keyed the mic on downwind and said "okay Danny you beautiful idiot, carb heat," and the tower lady said "carb heat approved, Five Two Bravo." Landing 1: good. Landing 2: bounced, went around, didn't die. Landing 3: good enough. Instructor cut my shirt (the Broncos one, RIP). Called Mom from the airplane before I even got out. She yelled at me for using a phone in an airplane. Then she cried. Then she asked if I was eating enough. Don't tell her I wrote that. Lesson: the airplane is way lighter with nobody in the other seat. Nobody tells you that. Somebody should tell you that.
She read it twice. The second time she laughed out loud in the empty hangar, one bark, and Marisol looked up from her bench and then decided not to.

Somebody should tell you that. Abby had, on the ramp, before she shut the door. Nobody had told him. She thought about Danny on downwind eleven years ago with the mic keyed, being heard, and herself this morning on the same downwind, talking the whole way, and nobody hearing any of it but Biscuit. Same habit, different airplane, different button. She found, sitting there on Marisol's stepladder, that she liked that. She'd expected to feel like she'd done something he had done. She felt like she'd done something, and he'd done it too.
She put the notebook down gently, like it was something that could be handed back.
She called her mother from the car.

Five rings, then voicemail. The recording was old, from when her mother still talked slower, and it said her full name, Lourdes Reyes, like she was checking in at a clinic. Jordan didn't leave a message. She put the phone face down on her leg, heater going, and looked out at Biscuit in her spot. Right door shut. She could see the top latch from here. Or thought she could. While she waited she ran the shutdown again in her head, since that's what her head did: mixture cutoff, mags off, master off, key on the dash, Hobbs written down, tie downs, gust lock.
Four minutes later the phone buzzed on her leg.

Mija. Her mother was breathing like she'd taken the stairs two at a time. Claire said it was today. I saw your name and I couldn't. I thought if I didn't pick up, then you were still up there and you were fine, and if I picked up it would be somebody else's voice. A long, long pause. Are you on the ground?
She was on the ground, Jordan told her. In the car. Parked.
Okay. She heard her mother sit down. The kitchen chair that scraped. Your brother called me from inside the airplane. I yelled at him.
Jordan said she knew. He'd written it down.

Nothing on the line for a while. Then a sound that could've been a laugh, or the other thing. Of course he did. Another long pause, the refrigerator humming in it. Jordan watched a fuel truck crawl by on the ramp, amber light, beeper, the driver eating a burrito with one hand and steering with the other. I'm still not getting in that airplane.
Next time, you call me before. So I can worry on time. Then, quiet enough that Jordan had to press the phone flat to her ear: Tell me how it was.

So she did, in order, like giving report at the ER doors: door open on rotation, three inches, then six, the noise, pattern, land, the latch. Then the hangar roofs going gold, the tower lady, Walt's eight fingers. Her mother didn't interrupt. At the door part she said Ay. Jordan kept going. When she got to the shirt tail her mother wanted to know which shirt, exactly. The one with the bleach on it? Good. That one was ugly.
